title: Forgiveness close
hookLine: sixty days on the hardest gift

lines: SIXTY DAYS ON THE HARDEST GIFT.
cards: A brother runs down a road toward the twin who cheated him. Genesis says it plainly, in the King James words: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept."
That was early in this block. Since then: a guard who reached out his hand, a bedtime prayer, a Jain phrase sent wide, a day of fasting, and a long list of people who are hard to forgive.
Sixty days on what this path called the hardest gift. Today it all gathers up, and then comes the one thing the whole block has been circling: let one thing go.

teach.b: First, what forgiveness isn't. Forgiving is not excusing: the wrong stays named as a wrong. It isn't the same as reconciling, which takes two people and happens only where it's safe.
And not yet is allowed. Second, the order.

A Jewish teaching said that for wrongs between people, you go to the person first. Jesus told the one bringing a gift to leave it at the altar and be reconciled first. A good apology owns the wrong and repairs it.
Third, the stories. Joseph wept aloud before his brothers. Esau ran.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at Ta'if, did not curse the town that drove him out. Angulimala stopped.
Each is a picture of something held, and a hand that opens.

Fourth, the times set aside: the Days of Awe and Yom Kippur, Kshamavani, Forgiveness Sunday, the Night of Power, the small nightly prayer before sleep, and yesterday's five answers, each in its own home.
So what does let it go mean, after all that? Not that the thing was fine. Not forgetting, or going back.

It means you stop carrying it everywhere you go. Paul's letter to the Colossians puts it in the King James words: "forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any".
A quarrel is real. And it can still be set down.

how: Some traditions mark forgiveness with a gesture of release, such as casting crumbs into water at Tashlich, asking forgiveness aloud at Kshamavani, or a bedtime prayer that forgives the day.

o: a real complaint that can still be set down
a grudge you must pretend never happened
a shouting match that has to end in a hug

games.q: sixty days of forgiveness — tap the pairs.
p: stop carrying it, not call it fine

s: letting it go means saying the wrong was okay
the wrong stays named as a wrong; letting go means you stop carrying it.
forgiving and reconciling are the same step
reconciling takes two people, and happens only where it's safe.
Genesis says Esau ran to meet Jacob and they wept
"and Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him… and they wept."

games.q: you've forgiven someone who hurt you, but being near them still isn't safe. what did this block say?
o: forgiving means you have to go back.
you can forgive and keep your distance.
you can't forgive until it's safe to return.
games.why: forgiving can be done alone; reconciling is a separate step, taken only where it's safe.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you've been carrying, a comment, a slight, a grudge with no one left to argue with, and name it silently as what it was.
Rest one hand palm up on your knee as if it sat there, and on each slow out-breath let the hand soften: not saying it was okay, just putting it down for now.
If it comes back, notice it and set it down again; if you pray, you can offer it in your own way.

wordCard.voice: Quarrel. Paul's word in Colossians for the real complaint that forbearing and forgiving can still set down. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: let it go. Sixty days on the hardest gift, gathered into three words. Tomorrow, a new question: awe.
